text: How does a car turn a corner without fighting its own wheels?
In every ninety-degree turn, the outside wheel rolls more than two metres farther than the inside one.
If both wheels were locked together, one tyre would have to scrub and skid.
The fix is a clever box of gears called the differential.
In a rear-wheel-drive car, the driveshaft spins a small pinion gear.
The pinion turns a big ring gear, sending the power out toward the wheels at ninety degrees, and slowing it down for extra torque.
Bolted to the ring gear is the carrier. Inside it sit small spider gears, and they mesh with two side gears, one for each axle.
Driving straight, the spider gears don't spin. The whole carrier turns as one, and both wheels roll at the same speed.
But in a turn, the spider gears start to rotate. They let the outside wheel speed up exactly as much as the inside wheel slows down.
There's one catch. An open differential sends equal torque to both wheels. Put one wheel on ice, and it just spins.
So engineers added limited-slip differentials, using clutches or special gears to send more power to the wheel with grip.
And that's how your car glides through every single corner.
